# War rockets (`war_rockets`)

<!-- generated by scripts/build_techtree.py from techtree/core/military.yaml — do not edit -->

- Category: Warfare, security & deterrence (`military`)
- Deps: needs gunpowder; helped by bloomery_iron, laws_of_motion
- Core idea: A rocket carries its own source of propulsion and gains momentum as gas escapes backwards. Chinese texts use the expression 'fire arrow' for more than one kind of projectile, making claims about the first rocket difficult to date. Iron-cased rockets became a distinctive feature of Mysore's forces under Haidar Ali and Tipu Sultan. British encounters with them helped inspire William Congreve's programme. Early military rockets were conspicuous and difficult to aim consistently. Their historical significance lies as much in the transmission of technology from South Asia to Europe as in their battlefield effects.
- Pitfalls:
  - Counting every reference to a fire arrow as evidence of a self-propelled rocket.
  - Attributing the military rocket to Congreve without accounting for earlier Chinese, Korean and Mysorean examples.
  - Treating spectacular contemporary accounts as measured evidence of accuracy or effectiveness.
- History: china: 13th c. – rockets certain (earlier 'fire arrows' from the 10th c. were mostly incendiary arrows shot from bows; the date of the first true rocket is disputed); 14th c. – multiple launchers in the Huolongjing; islamic: c. 1280 – Hasan al-Rammah describes rockets as 'Chinese arrows'; east_asia: 1448–1451 – Korean singijeon rockets and the hwacha multiple launcher; india: 1780–1799 – iron-cased Mysore rockets of Haidar Ali and Tipu Sultan; europe: 1380 – rockets reported at Chioggia; 1405 – Kyeser's Bellifortis; 1805–1807 – Congreve rockets copied from Mysore, used at Boulogne and Copenhagen; 1844 – Hale's spin-stabilised rocket
- Read:
  - Joseph Needham et al., Science and Civilisation in China, vol. 5 part 7: Military Technology: The Gunpowder Epic (1986)
  - Frank H. Winter, The First Golden Age of Rocketry (1990)
  - Roddam Narasimha, Rockets in Mysore and Britain, 1750–1850 A.D. (Bangalore lecture, 2 April 1985)
